intro: The spouse visa financial requirement is the most common reason partner applications are refused. Here’s how the £29,000 threshold works, what income and savings count, and who is exempt.
cardText: How the £29,000 threshold works, and what counts.

sections.heading: The spouse visa financial requirement in 2026
sections.text: Most new partner applications need a gross annual income of at least £29,000, shown through one or more of: employment, self-employment, pension, certain other income, or cash savings.

sections.heading: Using savings
sections.text: Savings above £16,000 can make up a shortfall in income. For a first application or extension, the shortfall is multiplied by 2.5. If you rely on savings alone, you need £16,000 plus 2.5 times the full £29,000, which is £88,500. Savings must usually have been held for at least 6 months.

sections.heading: Who is exempt?
sections.text: If your partner receives certain benefits, such as some disability or carer’s benefits, you don’t need to meet the £29,000 threshold. Instead you show “adequate maintenance”: that you can support yourselves without other public funds.

sections.heading: Evidence is everything
sections.text: The rules set out exactly which payslips, bank statements and letters you need, for which periods. Small gaps are the commonest reason for refusal, so we check every page.

faqs.q: What is the spouse visa financial requirement?
faqs.a: £29,000 a year for most new applications, from income, savings or both.

faqs.q: Can I combine income and savings?
faqs.a: Yes, in many cases, using the formula for savings above £16,000.

faqs.q: Does my income count if I’m the applicant?
faqs.a: If you’re already working in the UK with permission to work, your income can usually count.

title: Spouse Visa Financial Requirement 2026 | £29,000 Explained
description: The spouse visa financial requirement explained: the £29,000 threshold, using savings, the £88,500 savings-only figure, exemptions and evidence.
